name: TB-500

lead: TB-500 is the name research-peptide vendors use for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4, or a fragment of it. Lifters use it, often with BPC-157, for faster recovery of muscle and tendon injuries, and some claim skin and anti-ageing benefits.

Thymosin beta-4 binds actin and in animal models has been linked to angiogenesis, lower inflammation and better cell survival in injured tissue. Research on the full protein concerns wound, corneal and cardiac repair. Analysis of a veterinary TB-500 product found a short fragment (residues 17 to 23) rather than the full protein, and human evidence for the fragment is scarce.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and used in recovery stacks around injuries. What is in a given vial can differ by vendor.

Human safety data are lacking and product identity and purity are inconsistent. Pro-angiogenic activity is a theoretical concern in people with cancer risk. It is not an approved drug and thymosin beta-4 is prohibited by WADA.

angle.text: TB-500 is used, often with BPC-157, by lifters who want faster recovery from muscle and tendon injuries, and some claim skin and anti-ageing benefits. Quicker repair means more consistent training. Evidence is preclinical, and what vendors sell under the name varies.

lead: TB-500 is the name used by research-peptide suppliers for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4), a small protein found in most human cells, or for a fragment of it. Analytical chemistry work on a veterinary product called TB-500 found its key ingredient to be a short, N-terminally acetylated fragment of Tβ4 covering residues 17 to 23 (Ac-LKKTETQ), the region associated with actin binding, rather than the full-length protein [1][2]. Because the term is used loosely, what a given vendor sells under the name can differ.

People use TB-500 in the hope of faster recovery from tendon, muscle and joint injuries, and through that, more consistent training and a better physique. In sports-recovery and looksmaxxing communities it is most often paired with BPC-157 in what is nicknamed a 'Wolverine stack', and a smaller number of posters hope the pair may also help skin or facial structure [3][4][5][6]. The research on full-length Tβ4 concerns wound, corneal and cardiac repair; research on the shorter fragment in healthy people recovering from injury is almost absent, and reviews of injectable peptides describe the human evidence for TB-500 as scarce [7][8][9].

TB-500 is not an approved drug. Thymosin beta-4 is prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and the substance was at the centre of the Essendon supplements affair in Australian football, in which the Court of Arbitration for Sport in 2016 found 34 players guilty of using it [10][11]. Media and regulatory attention to the wider category of unapproved injectable peptides has grown since the mid-2020s, including a reported US policy announcement in 2026 on compounding of several such peptides [12].

paras: Thymosin beta-4 is encoded by the TMSB4X gene and is a major constituent of many cell types, reaching intracellular concentrations as high as 0.5 mM according to Wikipedia. Its best-characterised role is as the principal actin-sequestering protein: it forms a 1:1 complex with globular (G) actin and acts as a buffer for monomeric actin [10]. The sequence LKKTET, beginning at residue 17, is highly conserved among beta-thymosins and is often called the actin-binding motif [10].

A 2012 doping-control paper described a veterinary preparation called TB-500 that contained the peptide LKKTETQ with an artificial N-terminal acetylation, and noted that the preparation was claimed to promote endothelial cell differentiation, angiogenesis and keratinocyte migration [1]. A companion study synthesised the acetylated 17-23 fragment, identified it in TB-500, and described the product as suspected of doping potential [2]. Later reviews group TB-500 (described as a thymosin beta-4 fragment) with Tβ4 itself under a single heading when discussing peptides marketed to athletes [8][9].

The relationship between Tβ4 and TB-500 is a recurring source of confusion. Tβ4 is the full 43-44 amino-acid protein that appears in the medical literature, while the vendor product described in the doping-control papers is the short acetylated fragment, and later reviews group the two under one heading [10][1][2][8][9]. Wikipedia notes that Tβ4 is one of the most abundant proteins in many tissues and that the Wikipedia article itself is flagged for unsourced material in its section on proposed non-actin functions [10].

TB-500 is promoted in training communities for soft-tissue injuries, tendon and muscle tears and post-surgical recovery, and some posters also hope it may improve skin appearance, such as wrinkles, as part of peptide stacks [3][4][13]. It is typically sold as a research chemical.

Wikipedia reports that full-length Tβ4 has been tested in phase 2 trials in patients with pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa, where it accelerated repair and was safe and well tolerated, and in trials for dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy [10]. These trials concerned the protein or an acetylated form used as a medicine, not vendor products labelled TB-500.

On looksmax.org, TB-500 appears in threads about peptide stacks for recovery after surgery or gym injury, usually together with BPC-157, and posters report cycling both during recovery from operations [5]. One looksmax.org thread titled as a guide proposed using the pair to remodel cranial sutures and widen the cheekbones, claiming a 1.5 mm gain in width and a 10 per cent increase in jaw density on a DEXA scan, and describing the method as meant for people under 25 [6]. The thread's claims are the author's own and are not taken from a published trial.

Another looksmax.org thread asks whether TB-500 for muscle growth and recovery is worthwhile or 'cope' [14]. On T Nation, TB-500 is almost always mentioned alongside BPC-157 in training logs where lifters describe injecting both near an injured hamstring, knee or shoulder, sometimes within larger stacks that also include anabolic steroids and growth hormone [3][4][15].

Cell-culture and animal experiments have shown that Tβ4 can promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation, stem-cell maturation and cell survival and can lower production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [10]. In mice it has been reported to stimulate formation of new heart muscle cells from precursor cells in the heart's outer lining [10]. Wikipedia notes that these tissue-repair effects may not depend on intracellular actin binding, since the cells affected already have high levels of Tβ4; a role for extracellular receptors has been proposed [10].

An oxidised form, Tβ4 sulfoxide, was reported by a Glasgow group in 1999 to show anti-inflammatory effects on neutrophils [10]. Whether the shorter fragment sold as TB-500 reproduces the effects of the full protein has not been established. Orthopaedic reviews list TB-500, BPC-157 and GHK-Cu together as wound-healing peptides that act on angiogenesis, matrix remodelling and fibroblast activation, while noting a lack of clinical trials [16].

Reviews aimed at sports-medicine clinicians conclude that many unapproved peptides show favourable tissue-repair and metabolic outcomes in animals but that rigorous human safety data are scarce [8]. A 2026 primer for orthopaedic physicians evaluated BPC-157, Tβ4, TB-500 and other peptides and reported that findings were largely unvalidated in human trials [7]. A further 2026 review in the American Journal of Sports Medicine states that peptides in this group are often perceived as low risk despite an absence of efficacy or safety data for many of them [17].

A 2026 histopathological and biomechanical study in rats examined BPC-157 and TB-500 together in Achilles tendon healing; its details were not available in the abstract reviewed. The wider literature on Tβ4 in animals, summarised in older reviews, describes it as a multifunctional repair and regeneration peptide [18][19].

No completed, published controlled trial of TB-500 for tendon, muscle or appearance outcomes in healthy or injured people has been identified. A review of the field describes only preclinical data for the popular recovery peptides apart from small human case series [7][16].

One trial of the fragment is registered: NCT07487363, a phase 1/2 study of TB-500 (thymosin beta-4 17-23 fragment) for cardiovascular biomarkers in people with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (n=80), listed as recruiting from February 2026 [20]. Separate human trials exist for full-length thymosin beta-4, as noted above [10][21].

There are no systematic human safety data for vendor TB-500 products. A 2026 review of 'biohacking' injectables lists BPC-157, TB-500 and melanotan-II among unapproved peptides that lack established human safety profiles and describes potential risks including product contamination, impurities, inaccurate dosing, pathological angiogenesis and carcinogenesis [9]. A review of approved and unapproved peptide therapies similarly states that there is potential for serious harm because rigorous human safety data are scarce [8].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, notes that Tβ4 has been correlated with tumour metastatic potential and angiogenesis in some cancers, a dual role it describes as a reason for caution in regenerative use [22]. The relevance of this to TB-500 products has not been tested in humans.

Wikipedia states that thymosin beta-4 is considered performance-enhancing and is banned by WADA because it may aid soft-tissue recovery and allow higher training loads [10]. It featured in two Australian controversies in which large numbers of players at the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks (National Rugby League) and the Essendon Football Club (Australian Football League) were found to have been administered the substance in a programme organised by the sports scientist Stephen Dank, and were suspended [10].

Analytical chemists developed detection methods for TB-500 in horse urine and plasma from 2012 onwards, and later papers examined analytical issues such as adsorption losses of TB-500 during sample handling [1][2][23]. A review of doping-control analysis lists TB-500 among the peptides that testing laboratories must cover [24].

Thymosins were studied from the early 1960s as thymus-derived factors with immune effects, and Allan Goldstein's group prepared a partially purified calf thymus extract called thymosin fraction 5 in 1972, according to Grokipedia [22]. Wikipedia notes that thymosin beta-4 was the second peptide from this fraction to be fully sequenced and synthesised, after thymosin alpha-1, and that it was first thought to be a thymic hormone before being shown to be an actin-sequestering protein [10].

Reviews published in 2005 and 2010 framed Tβ4 as an actin-sequestering protein that 'moonlights' in tissue repair, setting the scientific background to later commercial interest [18][19]. The veterinary TB-500 preparation emerged in racehorse doping-control literature by 2012 [1].

In the Australian doping controversies of 2011 to 2016 the substance moved from laboratory interest into public view. Wikipedia reports that at Essendon, sports scientist Stephen Dank ran a 2011-2012 supplements programme in which players were injected with a product listed only as 'thymosin', which the Court of Arbitration for Sport later identified as the banned thymosin beta-4 [11]. The Australian Crime Commission published a report on organised crime and drugs in sport on 7 February 2013, and ASADA and the AFL began a joint investigation [11]. In 2015 the AFL Tribunal found 34 players not guilty, and WADA appealed to CAS; on 12 January 2016 CAS overturned the ruling and found them guilty of using thymosin beta-4, with two-year suspensions backdated to 31 March 2015 [11]. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed the players' appeal on 11 October 2016 [11].

At the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks, Wikipedia's account of the affair names the growth-hormone-releasing peptides CJC-1295 and GHRP-6, rather than thymosin, as the substances Dank admitted injecting; the club's coach Shane Flanagan received a 12-month ban in December 2013 and players accepted bans of up to 12 months in 2014 [25]. Wikipedia's thymosin beta-4 article nonetheless lists both clubs among the Australian scandals involving the peptide [10].

Basic research on Tβ4 spans several decades. A 2005 review framed it as an actin-sequestering protein that 'moonlights' in repairing injured tissue, and a 2010 review summarised animal studies of Tβ4 as a multifunctional repair and regeneration peptide [18][19]. A 2015 review covers its basic and clinical applications [21].

Wikipedia states that phase 2 trials of full-length Tβ4 in pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa reported faster healing and good tolerability, and that human eye trials reported improvement in dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy [10]. In mice, Tβ4 has been reported to stimulate new heart muscle cells from precursor cells [10]. These findings concern the full protein or its medical formulations rather than vendor TB-500, and no published study has compared them [10][7].

On T Nation, TB-500 is almost always mentioned alongside BPC-157, in logs where lifters describe injecting both near an injured hamstring, knee or shoulder [3][4][15]. Some posters list the two peptides among large stacks that also include anabolic steroids, growth hormone and other drugs [4]. One forum poster notes that a 'research chemical' defence might not protect someone prosecuted for possession of TB-500, with used needles as evidence [26].

Wikipedia's BPC-157 article reports that, in October 2026, the US Health Secretary announced that compounding pharmacies would be allowed to supply BPC-157 and several related peptides, including TB-500, for human use without FDA approval; the same article says health authorities continue to discourage use because of limited human safety data and that WADA banned BPC-157 in 2022 [12]. As that policy development is recent, readers should check current regulator pages for the present position.

A 2026 sports-medicine review states that peptides in this group are often perceived as low risk despite an absence of efficacy or safety data for many of them [17]. Elite-sport anti-doping bodies treat the peptide differently: testing laboratories have developed screening methods for TB-500 and related peptides in urine and plasma [23][24].

Low, Hu and Goldstein sequence and synthesise bovine thymosin beta-4, the second peptide from thymosin fraction 5 to be fully characterised. [10]
Glasgow researchers report anti-inflammatory effects of oxidised Tβ4 on neutrophils. [10]

On 12 January the Court of Arbitration for Sport finds 34 Essendon players guilty of using thymosin beta-4; the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismisses their appeal on 11 October. [11]
